sections.COMMENTS:
The Sicilian arc represents the interface between the allochthonous units of the Sicilian Fold and Thrust Belt (SFTB) overthrusted on the Hyblean margin. The SFTB forms the backbone of mainland Sicily and is part of the Maghrebian-Apennines orogenic belt, forming the broad central-western Mediterranean collisional plate boundary. The leading edge of this thrust system crops out onshore in its eastern portion between the cities of Gela and Catania; this section is confined to the east by the structures related to the subduction system of the Ionian basin and in its western portion between Capo Granitola and Sciacca. Its central section follows a broad southerly convex arc running for most of its length offshore the southern Sicilian coast (Gela Nappe). In western Sicily, the trend of the SFTB gradually turns to a NE-SW/NNE-SSW strike, forming a northward recess around the Saccense Meso-Cenozoic carbonate platform. This front eventually crosses the Sicily Channel along the Adventure Thrust Front (ATF), thus connecting with the thrust fronts outcropping on land in Tunisia. Offshore of the southern Sicily coast, to the east of the ATF, two N-S trending transpressional fault systems cut across the foreland faults, forming the Capo Granitola (CGFS) and Sciacca (SFS) fault systems (Ferranti et al., 2019). The latter, also known as the Belice-Sciacca Wrench Fault System (Argnani et al., 1986), is interpreted as the structure that separates two sectors of the Sicily Channel rift zone. The Sicilian-Maghrebian fold-and-thrust belt developed since early Miocene times in the framework of the ca. N-S directed Africa-Europe plate convergence and deformed rocks mostly belonging to the northern African paleomargin. This is characterized by carbonate platforms and interposed deep basins (Pelagian domain), involving in the deformation of Neogene-Quaternary foredeep deposits along the external fronts. Geological and geophysical subsurface data show that the SFTB is made up of two superposed structural levels: the shallower is a thin-skinned layer composed of thrust sheets involving deep-water rocks, overthrusted during the Miocene on the deeper layer, that in turn deforms the shallow-water platform carbonates of the Hyblean and Saccense units. From the late Miocene (Messinian), the lower level was deformed by deep-seated thrust ramps associated with long-wavelength anticlines that passively refolded the upper structural level (Oldow et al., 1990; Avellone et al., 2010; Catalano et al., 2013).
The most recent GPS solutions for the broad Sicily area, due to a denser network of stations, supply a greater detail for the area included between the Hyblean foreland and the Sicilian-Maghrebian chain in eastern Sicily (e.g., Devoti et al., 2017). At the regional scale, GPS data highlight an average N-S pattern of convergence across the outer fronts of the on-land sectors of the Sicilian-Maghrebian thrust system, in agreement with geological evidence of their recent activity testified by the deformation of Plio-Quaternary foredeep deposits and south of the Mt. Etna volcano, of late Pleistocene-Holocene marine and fluvial deposits.
Historical and instrumental catalogues show that in Sicily and surrounding areas, the most important seismic events are located in a few distinct sectors, including the Belice area, the Southern Tyrrhenian Sea offshore the northern Sicily coast, the Nebrodi and Peloritani mountain ranges, the Mount Etna, and the Hyblean regions. Only scattered and minor seismicity is observed in central Sicily (Caltanissetta Basin) and the Sicily Channel. The only destructive earthquakes in western Sicily occurred during the 1968 seismic sequence.
The work of Guidoboni et al. (2002) and Bottari et al. (2009), based on a detailed and systematic critical analysis of the archaeological data, highlighted the occurrence of at least two strong historical earthquakes that produced damage and destruction to the temples of Selinunte. These seismic events, dated to a period between the fourth and third centuries BCE and between the fourth and sixth century CE, respectively, are currently not included in the Italian seismic parametric catalogues that start at the year 1000. These events may have been produced by individual sources belonging to the SFTB or may be connected with the activity of the thrust fronts running between Castelvetrano and Capo Granitola. However, there are no indications of the causative seismic sources' magnitude and true location.
